name: Nation state
scope: The nation-state as an ideal and political model: a territorially bounded sovereign state ruled in the name of a community of citizens who identify as a nation, whose legitimacy comes from that nation's right to self-determination (national sovereignty) fused with the state's right to govern its territory free of outside interference (state sovereignty, Westphalia). It is the congruence ideal of Gellner: state borders should match the boundaries of the national community. Taken from Britannica's Nation-state and Sovereignty entries, the Stanford Encyclopedia's Nationalism entry and Weisband and Thomas's Political Culture and the Making of Modern Nation-States. It excludes nationalism as a whole (the sentiment, ethnic or religious nationalisms, which have their own articles), the individual states themselves (France, Israel) and the sovereignty of non-national polities such as tribes; and books that only use the phrase in a title or as a place name (US 'national, state and local' government manuals, NATO and WMD policy studies) or that argue against the nation-state (Hosein's critique from a caliphate view, the Executive Intelligence Review pamphlet) are not its own account.

keyFigures.role: Theorist of nationalism as the demand that each nation have its own political roof

summary: The nation-state is a sovereign, territorially bounded state ruled in the name of a community of citizens who see themselves as a nation. It fuses state sovereignty (governing its territory free of outside interference) with national sovereignty (the nation's right to govern itself, resting on popular consent), and aspires to borders that match the national community. The sources describe the model and its tensions with diversity, globalization and supranational bodies rather than prescribing policies, so most statements have no recorded position.

notes: Themes searched across all ten: the defining sources (Britannica nation-state, sovereignty, nationalism; SEP Nationalism; Weisband and Thomas) describe the model's two principles and its challenges, and state positions only on consent, national self-determination and the state itself. Citizenship, immigration, language, international bodies and economy are discussed descriptively, not as tenets, so are null. The local books that only match the phrase by title (US civics manuals, defence studies) and critics (Hosein, Executive Intelligence Review) were not used.
